lessonTitle: Turning, Milling and Drilling: Spindle Speed and Material Removal

blocks.text: A first-year student drills a 12 mm hole in mild steel with the drill press left at 3000 rev/min. The drill squeals, the tip turns blue and the hole is ruined. At that speed the cutting edge moves at about 113 m/min, several times what a high-speed steel drill can take in steel. Spindle speed is not a matter of feel: it follows from the cutting speed the tool allows and the diameter.

blocks.markdown: Three machine tools do most of the cutting in a workshop, and they differ in which part moves. In **turning** the workpiece rotates and a single-point tool moves along or across it. In **milling** a multi-tooth cutter rotates and the workpiece is fed past it. In **drilling** a rotating drill is fed axially into stationary work.

rows: Tool moves along or across the axis
Cylinders, cones, steps, threads, bores, faced ends
Workpiece table moves under the cutter
Flat faces, slots, pockets, keyways, gear teeth, profiles
Round holes; with reamers, boring and taps: finished holes and threads
blocks.caption: Main machine tool motions.

blocks.title: Cutting speed, feed and depth of cut
blocks.text: **Cutting speed** $v$ is the speed of the cutting edge relative to the work surface (m/min). **Feed** $f$ is how far the tool advances per revolution in turning (mm/rev). **Depth of cut** $d$ is the thickness of the layer removed, measured perpendicular to the feed (mm). The tool material and work material determine the allowable cutting speed.

blocks.markdown: The machine is set by spindle speed $N$ in rev/min, not cutting speed. At diameter $D$ (mm) the surface travels $\pi D$ mm each revolution, so $v=\pi D N/1000$ in m/min. Rearranged, $N=1000v/(\pi D)$. A larger diameter therefore needs a lower spindle speed to keep the same cutting speed.

blocks.caption: Spindle speed N (rev/min) for cutting speed v (m/min) and workpiece or cutter diameter D (mm).

blocks.title: Spindle speed for a turned diameter
blocks.prompt: A mild steel bar of diameter 60 mm is to be turned at a cutting speed of 90 m/min. What spindle speed is needed?

steps.text: Write the formula with v in m/min and D in mm.
Evaluate the denominator: pi x 60 = 188.5, then 90 000/188.5.
Choose the nearest available lathe speed, for example 475 rev/min, and check the cutting speed it gives is acceptable.

blocks.answer: About 477 rev/min; the machine would be set to the nearest available speed.

blocks.caption: Material removal rate in turning for cutting speed v (m/min), feed f (mm/rev) and depth of cut d (mm). The factor 1000 converts metres to millimetres. Time to machine a length L is t = L/(f N).

blocks.title: MRR and machining time
blocks.prompt: A roughing cut on the bar uses $v=120$ m/min, $f=0.25$ mm/rev and $d=2.5$ mm. Find the material removal rate, and the machining time for a 150 mm length at 477.5 rev/min.

steps.text: Machining time: length divided by feed rate (f N = 0.25 x 477.5 = 119.4 mm/min).

blocks.answer: MRR is 75 cm^3/min and the pass takes about 1.26 minutes.

blocks.markdown: **Trade-offs.** MRR rises in proportion to each of $v$, $f$ and $d$. Roughing uses a large depth of cut and feed to remove material quickly, within the power and rigidity of the machine and the strength of the tool. Finishing uses a small depth and fine feed to meet tolerance and surface finish. Cutting speed has a strong effect on tool life; depth of cut and feed have a smaller effect on tool life and surface finish respectively.

items: Axisymmetric shapes (shafts, bushes, spigots, threads): turning.
Flat faces, slots, pockets and keyways on prismatic blocks: milling.
Round holes: drilling, finished with reaming or boring.
Large hole in a part that rotates easily on a lathe: bore it, which also gives concentricity.
Features on the same set-up are made together to preserve alignment.

blocks.markdown: **Choosing between turning and milling.** The question is which motion can generate the feature. Features concentric with an axis are produced by rotating the work. Features that are flat, offset or angular to the part axis require a rotating cutter. Many parts need both, so the process plan puts as many features as possible in one set-up.

blocks.title: Rotating work or rotating cutter?
blocks.text: If the feature is a surface of revolution about the part's axis, turn it; if it is a plane, slot or pocket, mill it; if it is a round hole, drill it. Rotational speed is set from the allowable cutting speed and the diameter of the work (turning) or of the cutter (milling and drilling).

blocks.title: Check the units
blocks.text: Cutting speed is in m/min but diameter is in mm, so the factor 1000 is essential. Always compute the cutting speed that a chosen spindle speed produces and compare it with the recommended range for the tool and material.

points: Turning rotates the workpiece, milling rotates the cutter and drilling rotates the drill; the feed motion differs in each.
Spindle speed is N = 1000 v / (pi D), and MRR in turning is 1000 v f d in mm^3/min.
Choose turning for surfaces of revolution, milling for flats, slots and pockets, and drilling for round holes, combining operations in one set-up where possible.

questions.stem: The cutting speed for a tool and material is fixed. If the workpiece diameter is doubled, what happens to the required spindle speed?

distractorRationale.b: The spindle speed is inversely proportional to diameter.
distractorRationale.c: The spindle speed depends on diameter for a given cutting speed.
distractorRationale.d: There is no squared relation in $N=1000v/(\pi D)$.

questions.explanation: Since $N=1000v/(\pi D)$, the speed is inversely proportional to the diameter. Larger diameter means more surface travel per revolution, so fewer revolutions per minute are needed.

questions.stem: In a turning operation the depth of cut is doubled with cutting speed and feed unchanged. What is the effect on material removal rate?

distractorRationale.b: MRR is proportional to depth of cut, so it increases.
distractorRationale.c: MRR depends directly on depth of cut.
distractorRationale.d: MRR is linear in depth, not quadratic.

questions.explanation: Material removal rate is $1000vfd$, which is directly proportional to each factor. Doubling the depth of cut therefore doubles the rate, provided the machine has the power and rigidity.

questions.stem: A stepped shaft with a 30 mm and a 22 mm diameter section must be produced from round bar. Which process is the natural choice?

distractorRationale.b: Milling is used for flat and prismatic features, not for turned diameters.
distractorRationale.c: Drilling makes holes, not external steps.
distractorRationale.d: Grinding flats does not generate cylinders.

questions.explanation: The shaft is a surface of revolution, which a lathe generates by rotating the work against a single-point tool. Milling is used for flats and slots.

questions.stem: A shaft needs a rectangular keyway 6 mm wide and 3.5 mm deep along part of its length. Which process is most suitable?

distractorRationale.b: Turning cannot cut a slot parallel to the axis.
distractorRationale.d: Facing makes the end flat, not a slot along the side.

questions.explanation: A slot is a prismatic feature made by a rotating cutter traversing along the shaft. The lathe makes surfaces concentric with the axis, so a keyway is milled.

questions.stem: Which pairing of rotating part and feeding part is correct for milling?

options.text: The cutter rotates and the workpiece is fed past it
The workpiece rotates and a single-point tool is fed along it
The drill rotates and feeds into stationary work
Both cutter and workpiece are stationary

questions.correctOptionText: The cutter rotates and the workpiece is fed past it

distractorRationale.d: Cutting needs relative motion between tool and work.

questions.explanation: In milling a multi-tooth cutter rotates while the table moves the workpiece into it. This arrangement contrasts with turning, where the workpiece rotates.

questions.stem: A 25 mm diameter bar is turned at a cutting speed of 40 m/min. What spindle speed, in rev/min, is needed?
questions.explanation: The speed is $N=1000\times40/(\pi\times25)=509.3$ rev/min. A machine speed of about 500 rev/min would be selected.

questions.stem: A turning pass uses a cutting speed of 200 m/min, feed 0.3 mm/rev and depth of cut 1.5 mm. What is the material removal rate in cm$^3$/min?
questions.explanation: The rate is $1000\times200\times0.3\times1.5=9.0\times10^{4}$ mm^3/min. Dividing by 1000 gives 90 cm^3/min.

questions.stem: A 180 mm length of a shaft is turned in one pass at a feed of 0.15 mm/rev and a spindle speed of 600 rev/min. How long does the pass take, in minutes?
questions.explanation: The feed rate is $0.15\times600=90$ mm/min. The time is $180/90=2.0$ min.

questions.stem: A flanged bush has an outer cylindrical surface, a central bore, a flat machined on the side of the flange and four holes on a bolt circle. State which machine tool you would use for each feature and justify, and say how you would limit the number of set-ups.
markingGuide: Outer cylinder and bore: turning (surfaces of revolution about the axis)
Four holes on bolt circle: drilling (on a drill press or in the milling machine)
Justification linked to which part rotates and which feature the motion produces
Sets-up limited by doing turned features together and using the same datum for milled and drilled features
questions.explanation: Each feature is matched to the process that generates it: rotation of the work for concentric surfaces, a rotating cutter for flats and a drill for holes. Combining features in one set-up preserves alignment and saves time.

questions.stem: Explain how cutting speed, feed and depth of cut each affect material removal rate in turning, and why a roughing cut and a finishing cut use different values.
markingGuide: MRR is proportional to speed, feed and depth of cut (MRR = 1000 v f d)
Roughing uses large depth and feed to remove material quickly, limited by machine power and rigidity
Finishing uses small depth and fine feed to meet tolerance and surface finish
Cutting speed is limited by tool material and tool life
Notes the trade-off between productivity and finish or tool life
questions.explanation: All three parameters multiply, so the increase of any raises the rate, but each has limits from machine capability, tool life and surface requirements. Hence roughing prioritises removal and finishing prioritises accuracy.
